terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Run the fares here, and print a variable to see what it holds.

tasks.title: Price the return ticket
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `Fares.java`, make an `int` called `returnFarePence`: two single fares, less 40 pence for buying both at once. The single fare is in `singleFarePence`, in pence.

Check runs your Task 1 lines with other fares in place of the one at the top and reads `returnFarePence`.
nextSteps: Read the numbers at the top of `main`: the fares are in whole pence.
Under `// Task 1`, make `returnFarePence` with the type for whole numbers.
On the right of `=`, write the sum with the name `singleFarePence`.
Print it and run `java Fares.java` to see the price.
hints: Two single fares is the fare times two. Then the 40 pence come off.
Java multiplies before it adds or subtracts, as in maths. Brackets change that, so only use them where you mean them.
The line has the shape `int returnFarePence = singleFarePence * ... - ...;`.

tasks.title: Count the full trips
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, `queue` people wait on the quay and the boat takes `seats` people a trip. Make an `int` called `fullTrips`: how many full boatloads the queue fills. Then make an `int` called `leftOver`: how many people are still on the quay after those full trips.

Check runs your Task 2 lines with queues and boats of its own, including a queue smaller than the boat and one that fills it exactly, and reads both.
nextSteps: Work out one example on paper: 100 people, 48 seats a trip.
Read the part of the lesson about dividing two ints.
Make `fullTrips` with the division that drops the rest.
Make `leftOver` with the operator that gives the rest.
hints: Dividing one `int` by another gives an `int`: the whole number of times, with the rest dropped. Here that is exactly what you want.
The rest of a division has its own operator in Java, `%`. `7 % 3` is 1.
The two lines have the shapes `int fullTrips = queue / ...;` and `int leftOver = queue % ...;`.

docs.title: Integer division and remainder in the Java language

tasks.title: Work out the average crossing
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, make a `double` called `averagePerCrossing`: `passengersToday` divided by `crossingsToday`, keeping the part after the point.

Check runs your Task 3 lines with numbers of its own, some whose average has a part after the point, and reads `averagePerCrossing`.
nextSteps: Write the division into a `double` and print it.
Run it: with 57 passengers over 12 crossings, does the answer look right?
Read the part of the lesson about why a `double` on the left is not enough.
Make one of the two numbers a `double` before the division.
hints: Both numbers are `int`s, so Java divides them as whole numbers first and only then stores the answer in the `double`.
A cast, `(double)` in front of a value, turns it into a `double`. Once one side of the division is a `double`, Java divides with decimals.
The line has the shape `double averagePerCrossing = (double) passengersToday / ...;`.

docs.title: Casting conversions in the Java language

tasks.title: Number the ticket
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 4`, make a `long` called `ticketNumber`: the date code times 100000, plus the ticket of the day. Ticket 57 on `20261123` is `2026112300057`. The two are in `dateCode` and `ticketOfDay`.

Check runs your Task 4 lines with dates and tickets of its own and reads `ticketNumber`.
nextSteps: Make `ticketNumber` as a `long` with the sum, and print it.
Compare what it prints with the example in the task.
Read the part of the lesson about how big an `int` can get.
Make the multiplication happen in `long`, not only the result.
hints: A thirteen digit number does not fit in an `int`, which is why the task asks for a `long`.
Storing the result in a `long` is not enough: `dateCode * 100000` is worked out first, as two `int`s, and it overflows before it reaches the `long`.
Make one side of the multiplication a `long`: write `100000L`, with an L, or put `(long)` in front of `dateCode`.
